subjective.question: Write down the functions of the cell wall.
subjective.answer: The cell wall performs the following functions: 1. Protection: It protects the cell against mechanical injury and against the entry of pathogens.

subjective.question: Shape: It gives a definite shape to the cell.
Mechanical support: It provides strength and support to the cell and to the whole plant body, helping it to stand upright.
Prevention of bursting: It prevents the cell from bursting when it absorbs excess water in a hypotonic environment.
Control of growth: Its controlled stretching regulates the rate and direction of cell growth.
Communication: Plasmodesmata passing through the cell walls of adjacent plant cells allow transport and communication between them.
Defence and storage: Specialized walls (e.g. with lignin or suberin) act as barriers, and in seeds the wall may store food material.
Define Philadelphia chromosome.
subjective.answer: The Philadelphia chromosome is an abnormally short chromosome 22 formed by a reciprocal translocation between chromosome 9 and chromosome 22, written as t(9;22). In this translocation, the ABL1 gene from chromosome 9 joins the BCR gene on chromosome 22, forming a fusion gene called BCR-ABL. This fusion gene produces an abnormal tyrosine kinase enzyme that remains permanently active and stimulates uncontrolled division of white blood cells. The Philadelphia chromosome is the characteristic chromosomal abnormality of chronic myeloid leukemia (CML).

subjective.question: What are histones? Describe the role of histone H1 in chromatin packing.
subjective.answer: Histones are small, basic (positively charged) proteins that package DNA inside the nucleus. DNA is negatively charged, so it wraps tightly around a histone octamer made of two copies each of H2A, H2B, H3 and H4. The DNA wrapped around this octamer forms a nucleosome, the basic unit of chromatin. Histone H1 is called the linker histone. It binds the linker DNA at the points where DNA enters and leaves the nucleosome and seals it in place. H1 promotes folding of the nucleosome chain into a thicker 30 nm chromatin fibre, so the chromatin becomes tightly packed and less accessible for transcription.

subjective.question: What is prophase? Describe the main events of prophase.
subjective.answer: Prophase is the first and longest phase of mitosis. The main events of prophase are: 1. The chromatin fibres condense and become visible as distinct chromosomes under the microscope. 2. Each chromosome consists of two sister chromatids joined at the centromere. 3. The nucleolus gradually disappears. 4. The centrosomes move towards opposite poles of the cell.

subjective.question: Spindle fibres made of microtubules begin to form between the poles. Towards the end of prophase, the nuclear envelope breaks down and the spindle fibres attach to the chromosomes.
Explain Mendelian and non-Mendelian inheritance with examples.
subjective.answer: Mendelian inheritance follows the patterns described by Mendel. A trait is controlled by a single gene with two alleles, one of which is completely dominant over the other. It produces definite ratios, e.g. 3:1 in a monohybrid cross and 9:3:3:1 in a dihybrid cross. Examples: tall and dwarf plants of pea, purple and white pea flowers. Non-Mendelian inheritance includes all patterns that do not follow Mendel's simple rules. Its main types are: 1. Incomplete dominance: the heterozygote is intermediate, e.g. pink flowers from red and white snapdragons. 2. Codominance: both alleles are fully expressed, e.g. AB blood group in humans. 3. Multiple alleles: a gene has more than two alleles, e.g. the ABO blood group system. 4. Polygenic (multifactorial) inheritance: many genes act together, e.g. height and skin colour in humans. 5. Sex-linked inheritance: genes carried on sex chromosomes, e.g. colour blindness and haemophilia.

subjective.question: Pleiotropy and epistasis: one gene affecting many traits, or one gene masking another gene.
Describe the experiment of T. H. Morgan with an example.
subjective.answer: T. H. Morgan worked on the fruit fly, Drosophila melanogaster. He crossed a red-eyed female with a white-eyed male. In the F1 generation all flies had red eyes, showing that red eye colour is dominant. When F1 flies were crossed, the F2 generation showed a 3:1 ratio of red-eyed to white-eyed flies, but all the white-eyed flies were males. Morgan concluded that the gene for eye colour is located on the X chromosome, i.e. inheritance can be sex-linked. This work gave the first concrete evidence that genes are carried on chromosomes, and Morgan also discovered that genes present on the same chromosome are linked and are inherited together.

subjective.question: Explain how environmental factors affect allelic expression.
subjective.answer: The phenotype of an organism is produced by the interaction of its genotype with the environment, so environmental factors can change the way alleles are expressed. Examples: 1. Temperature: In Himalayan rabbits and Siamese cats, the enzyme (tyrosinase) that produces dark pigment is temperature-sensitive. It works only in the cooler parts of the body, so the ears, nose, feet and tail become dark while the warmer body remains light-coloured. 2. Soil pH: Hydrangea plants produce blue flowers in acidic soil and pink flowers in alkaline soil, although the genotype is the same. 3. Light and nutrition: A genetically tall plant remains dwarf in poor soil or without light, and human height and intelligence are also influenced by nutrition and upbringing. Thus the same genotype can produce a range of phenotypes under different environments; this range is called the norm of reaction.

subjective.question: What is non-disjunction? Explain it with examples.
subjective.answer: Non-disjunction is the failure of chromosomes to separate properly during meiosis. It may occur in meiosis I, when homologous chromosomes fail to separate, or in meiosis II, when sister chromatids fail to separate. As a result, gametes are produced with an extra chromosome (n + 1) or with a missing chromosome (n - 1). Fertilization of such gametes produces aneuploid individuals. Examples: 1. Down syndrome: trisomy of chromosome 21 (47 chromosomes). 2. Klinefelter syndrome: 47, XXY in males. 3. Turner syndrome: 45, XO in females (monosomy of the X chromosome). Most other aneuploidies are lethal and cause miscarriage.

subjective.question: Name and briefly describe the techniques used for gene mapping.
subjective.answer: The main techniques used for mapping genes on chromosomes are: 1. Linkage (genetic) mapping: Based on recombination frequencies between genes; the greater the distance between two genes, the higher the recombination frequency. Distances are measured in centimorgans. 2. Cytogenetic mapping: Genes are located on specific bands of chromosomes using staining techniques and microscopic examination of deletions and translocations. 3. Physical mapping: The actual distance between genes is measured in base pairs, using methods such as restriction mapping, fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) and sequence-tagged sites (STS). 4. Radiation hybrid mapping: Chromosomes are broken by radiation and the fragments are studied in hybrid cells to determine the order and distance of markers.

subjective.question: What is multifactorial inheritance? Give examples.
subjective.answer: Multifactorial inheritance is the inheritance of traits that are controlled by many genes (polygenes) acting together with environmental factors. Such traits do not show simple Mendelian ratios; instead they show continuous variation in a population. Examples of multifactorial traits are height, weight, skin colour and intelligence in humans. Many common human disorders are also multifactorial, e.g. diabetes mellitus, heart diseases, hypertension, cleft lip and palate, and schizophrenia. Their risk increases when both genetic susceptibility and environmental factors (diet, lifestyle, infections) are present.

subjective.question: Why are male honey bees haploid? What is meant by haplodiploidy?
subjective.answer: Honey bees show haplodiploidy, a system of sex determination in which males develop from unfertilized eggs and females develop from fertilized eggs. The queen lays two types of eggs: fertilized eggs (diploid, 2n = 32) develop into females (queens and workers), while unfertilized eggs develop by parthenogenesis into males, called drones. The drones therefore carry only one set of chromosomes (n = 16) and are haploid. A drone produces sperms by mitosis, not by meiosis, because its cells are already haploid.

subjective.question: What is polyploidy? Give an example from plants.
subjective.answer: Polyploidy is the condition in which an organism has more than two complete sets of chromosomes in its cells. It is common in plants and is produced by failure of cell division after chromosome replication, or by hybridization followed by chromosome doubling. The cultivated strawberry (Fragaria x ananassa) is an octaploid, having eight sets of chromosomes (8n = 56). Another example is bread wheat, which is hexaploid (6n). Polyploid plants are often larger, have bigger fruits and are more vigorous, so polyploidy is widely used in crop improvement.

subjective.question: Define deamination.
subjective.answer: Deamination is the removal of an amino group (-NH2) from a molecule. In DNA, spontaneous deamination of nitrogenous bases is an important source of mutation: deamination of cytosine produces uracil, and deamination of adenine produces hypoxanthine. If such changes are not repaired, they cause point mutations in the next replication. In metabolism, deamination of amino acids takes place in the liver, where the removed amino group is converted into ammonia and then into urea for excretion.

subjective.question: Name and describe the types of deoxyribonucleotides found in DNA.
subjective.answer: DNA contains four types of deoxyribonucleotides. Each deoxyribonucleotide is made of a deoxyribose sugar, a phosphate group and one nitrogenous base. The four types are: 1. Deoxyadenosine monophosphate (dAMP) - contains adenine. 2. Deoxyguanosine monophosphate (dGMP) - contains guanine. 3. Deoxycytidine monophosphate (dCMP) - contains cytosine. 4. Deoxythymidine monophosphate (dTMP) - contains thymine. Adenine and guanine are purines (double-ring bases), while cytosine and thymine are pyrimidines (single-ring bases).

subjective.question: Differentiate between the different domains (activities) of DNA polymerase.
subjective.answer: DNA polymerase is not a single-function enzyme; its different domains carry out different activities: 1. 5' to 3' polymerase activity (polymerase domain): It adds deoxyribonucleotides to the free 3'-OH end of the growing strand and synthesizes new DNA in the 5' to 3' direction. 2. 3' to 5' exonuclease activity (proofreading domain): It removes a wrongly incorporated nucleotide from the 3' end, so the enzyme can proofread and correct its own mistakes during replication. 3. 5' to 3' exonuclease activity: Present in DNA polymerase I; it removes RNA primers and damaged DNA segments ahead of the enzyme (nick translation). In DNA polymerase III, additional parts increase efficiency: the sliding clamp keeps the enzyme attached to DNA (processivity), and the clamp loader loads the clamp onto DNA. The Klenow fragment of DNA polymerase I retains the polymerase and 3' to 5' exonuclease activities but lacks the 5' to 3' exonuclease activity.

subjective.question: Describe the components and structure of DNA.
subjective.answer: DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is made of repeating units called nucleotides. Each nucleotide has three components: a deoxyribose sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base (adenine, thymine, guanine or cytosine). Two polynucleotide strands wind around each other to form a double helix. The strands are antiparallel and are held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases: adenine pairs with thymine through two hydrogen bonds, and guanine pairs with cytosine through three hydrogen bonds. According to Chargaff's rule, the amount of adenine equals thymine and the amount of guanine equals cytosine. This complementary structure allows DNA to store genetic information and to copy it accurately during replication.

subjective.question: Name and describe the different types of RNA.
subjective.answer: The three main types of RNA are: 1. Messenger RNA (mRNA): It is formed from DNA during transcription and carries the genetic message, in the form of codons, from the nucleus to the ribosome for protein synthesis. 2. Transfer RNA (tRNA): It carries amino acids to the ribosome. It has an anticodon that pairs with the codon of mRNA, so the amino acids are joined in the correct sequence. 3. Ribosomal RNA (rRNA): It is a structural and functional part of the ribosome, the site of protein synthesis, and helps in joining amino acids into a polypeptide chain. In addition, small nuclear RNAs (snRNA) take part in processing of mRNA, and micro RNAs (miRNA) regulate gene expression.

subjective.question: Differentiate between traditional and modern biotechnology.
subjective.answer: Traditional biotechnology is the use of living organisms in their natural form, practised for thousands of years. It includes fermentation for making bread, yogurt, cheese and beverages, and selective breeding of plants and animals to improve desired characters. No direct change is made in the genes of the organism. Modern biotechnology is based on recombinant DNA technology and genetic engineering, developed since the 1970s. Genes are isolated, cut, joined and transferred between organisms in the laboratory. It includes gene cloning, production of insulin and vaccines by genetically modified bacteria, tissue culture, monoclonal antibodies and transgenic plants and animals. Modern biotechnology is precise and fast compared with traditional methods.

subjective.question: What are vectors? Describe the features of a good cloning vector and give examples.
subjective.answer: A vector is a DNA molecule that is used to carry a foreign gene into a host cell, where the gene can be copied or expressed. A good cloning vector should have: 1. An origin of replication, so it can multiply inside the host cell. 2. A selectable marker gene (e.g. antibiotic resistance), so cells containing the vector can be identified. 3. One or more unique restriction sites (a multiple cloning site) where the foreign DNA can be inserted. 4. Small size, so it can be easily introduced into the host cell. Examples of vectors are plasmids (small circular DNA of bacteria, the most commonly used vectors), bacteriophage lambda, cosmids, bacterial artificial chromosomes (BACs) and yeast artificial chromosomes (YACs). The Ti plasmid of Agrobacterium is used for transferring genes into plants.
